To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the residual stress fields at surfaces of alumina hip joint heads can be detected by a variety of stress probes and that the spatial resolution of the detected residual stress fields depends critically on the choice of the stress probe.

(1) the in-depth and in-plane responses of photo- and electron-stimulated stress probes have been modeled in order to assess them in terms of their ability to assess the highly graded residual stresses generated at the surface layer of alumina hip joint components; and (2) the in-plane response function of an electro-stimulated stress probe has been shown to enable the assessment of residual stresses with a spatial resolution of the order of the nanometers.

the in-depth and in-plane spatial resolutions of photo-stimulated luminecence probes are in the tens of micrometers and tens of nanometers, respectively, whereas those of electron-stimulated luminesscence probes are in tens of nanometers in both dimensions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel stress probes and the quantitative analysis of their response functions in the case of alumina hip joint.
the development of a novel methodology to quantify residual stresses in the surface layer of alumina hip prostheses.
the development of new techniques and methods to assess surface residual stress in alumina hip joints.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of electro-stimulated stress probes, in particular the F(+) center, is the most suitable choice in order to obtain a reliable assessment of the residual stress field at the surface of the alumina femoral heads.

the use of electro-stimulated stress probes, as opposed to photo-stimulated ones, would be preferable in the case of highly graded stress fields, such as those encountered at the surface of the alumina hip joints.
the F(+) center luminescence probe is the only one able to detect the highly non-uniform residual stresses at the surface of an alumina hip joint.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of electro-stimulated Raman spectroscopy, which is the only probe that can detect the stress in a volume of the order of the nanometers, can be used to detect the stress in the surface layer of alumina hip joint, but only when the stress is high enough to induce a measurable shift of the Raman band.
the use of electron-stimulated lumine-scence is the most promising method to detect and map residual stresses at the surface of ceramic hip implants.
, in the presence of a highly graded residual stress field, the choice of the probe is a key factor to obtain quantitative and spatially resolved information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a confocal probe, such as the electro-stimulating probe, is mandatory for the accurate mapping of residual stresses at the surface of ceramic components.
residual stress fields at alumina surfaces can be quantitatively detected with a high spatial resolution and a high sensitivity by using electron-activated luminescence probes.
, when using photo-stimulated stress probes, the spatial resolution of stress measurements can be strongly affected by averaging effects.
